title: Clean tile grout
intro: Grey or blackened grout in the bathroom: bring it back with baking soda or a grout cleaner.

steps.t: Open the window and put your gloves on. If the tiles are wet, dry them first with a cloth.
Mix baking soda with a little water into a thick paste, like toothpaste. Or use a grout cleaner instead.
steps.w: Never mix different cleaners, especially bleach with acidic products: it gives off toxic gas.

steps.t: Work the paste into the grout lines with the toothbrush. Spray cleaners go straight onto the grout.
Leave it to work: the paste loosens the dirt while you wait. With a cleaner, follow the time on the label.
steps.label: Contact time

steps.t: Scrub along each line with the stiff brush in short, firm strokes, one section at a time.
Rinse with the sponge and clean water, wringing it often, until there's no white residue left.
Look at the grout in good light: it should be back to its original colour, with no black specks.
steps.q: Is the grout evenly light again?
steps.fix: Repeat paste, wait and scrub on the dark areas. For black mould specks use a mould remover, on its own.

steps.t: Dry the tiles and grout with the cloth.
Want to protect it? Let the grout dry properly, at least a couple of hours. Otherwise you're done.
steps.label: Drying

steps.t: Run the grout pen or sealer along the lines and wipe any smudges off the tiles straight away.

tips: No vinegar or acid cleaners on marble or natural stone: they etch the surface. Use baking soda or neutral cleaners.
Squeegee the walls and screen after every shower: the grout stays clean for much longer.
If the grout is crumbling or missing, cleaning won't fix it: it needs raking out and regrouting.

title: Replace a shower head or hose
intro: Limescale-clogged shower head or a leaking hose: swap them in a quarter of an hour, no plumber.

steps.t: Turn the mixer off firmly and lay a cloth in the shower tray: it protects the finish if something drops.
Unscrew the shower head or handset anticlockwise by hand. If it's stuck, use the wrench wrapped in the cloth.
If you're replacing the hose too, unscrew it from the mixer or wall outlet, again anticlockwise.
Clean the threads with the toothbrush and a little vinegar, removing limescale and any old washers left inside.
Put a new washer in each nut of the hose, sitting flat at the bottom: without one it will leak.
steps.q: Is there a flat washer in each nut?
steps.fix: Push it in flat with a finger; if it's twisted or split, use a new one of the same size.

steps.t: Screw the hex-nut end of the hose onto the mixer; the cone end usually goes to the handset.
Screw it on by hand as far as it goes, then at most a quarter turn with the wrench wrapped in the cloth.
Turn the water on and watch the joints for a minute, hot first and then cold.
steps.fix: Tighten another eighth of a turn. If it still drips, unscrew it and check the washer sits flat.

tips: For limescale, soak the head in white vinegar for an hour, then rub the rubber nozzles with your fingers.
Fixed head with no washer? Wrap 4-5 turns of PTFE tape clockwise round the thread before screwing it on.
Fittings are almost always a standard half-inch: if in doubt, take the old part to the shop.

title: Reseal a shower or bath
intro: Black or peeling sealant around the shower or bath: strip it out and lay a clean, watertight bead.

steps.t: Cut along both edges of the old sealant with the knife, holding the blade almost flat.
steps.w: Go gently on acrylic or enamelled baths and trays: the blade scratches easily.

steps.t: Grab one end of the bead and peel it away slowly, in one piece if you can.
Scrape off what's left with the plastic scraper until tiles and tray feel smooth.
Wipe the joint with a cloth and alcohol: it lifts the last residue and soap so the new sealant sticks.
Let everything dry with the window open: the joint must be dry right to the bottom.
steps.label: Drying
steps.q: Is the joint dry, clean and free of old sealant?
steps.fix: Wait longer or dry it with a hairdryer on low: sealant won't stick to damp and soon turns black.

steps.t: Tape both sides of the gap, leaving about [[3 mm]] of surface on each side, pressed down firmly.
Cut the nozzle at an angle, a bit wider than the gap, and run one continuous bead at a steady pace.
Smooth it in one pass with the tool or a finger dipped in soapy water, pressing lightly.
Pull the tape off straight away while the sealant is wet: slowly, at an angle away from the joint.
Check the bead along its whole length, especially in the corners.
steps.q: Is the bead continuous, with no holes or gaps?
steps.fix: Fill them now with a little sealant while it's wet and smooth again with a soapy finger.

steps.t: Let the sealant cure for 24 hours without using the shower, with the room aired.
steps.label: Curing

tips: Bath: fill it with water before sealing and empty it once cured, so the bead doesn't tear when the bath is used.
Use sanitary silicone with fungicide; a vinegar smell while it cures is normal, so keep the window open.
If the gap is wider than [[10 mm]], push in a foam backer rod first, then seal over it.
